task: Estimate whether a cable run is short enough for its protective device to trip quickly in a fault, and check voltage drop separately.
condition: Given cable size, length, supply voltage and device rating, using rounded teaching figures, with real designs checked by qualified people against the maker's tables and local rules.
standard: The learner calculates loop resistance and fault current for a run, compares it to the device trip level, and proposes a fix when the run is too long.

modules.title: The fault loop
modules.intro: In a fault, current runs out along one conductor and back along another. That round trip is the fault loop, and its resistance decides how big the fault current gets.
points: Loop length is twice the cable length, because current goes out and comes back.
Resistance rises with length and falls as the conductor gets thicker.
Less fault current means a protective device may trip slowly or not at all.
modules.example: Take a copper cable of 2.5 mm² and 40 m. Use 0.0225 ohm square millimetres per metre for copper (a rounded teaching figure, as are all the numbers in this lesson). The loop resistance is 2 × 0.0225 × 40 ÷ 2.5 = 1.8 ÷ 2.5 = 0.72 ohms. Doubling the length to 80 m would double this to 1.44 ohms. Halving the conductor to 1.25 mm² would also double it. Length and size pull in opposite directions.
modules.activity: Calculate loop resistance for three lengths of 2.5 mm² cable: 20 m, 40 m and 60 m. Plot or list the results and describe the pattern.
modules.standard: Learner uses the loop formula correctly and describes the effect of length and size.

modules.title: Fault current and trip level
modules.intro: Once you have the loop resistance, the basic rule current = voltage ÷ resistance gives the fault current. Compare it with what the device needs to trip fast.
points: Fault current is supply voltage divided by loop resistance in this simple model.
A device trips fast only above a trip level, often several times its rating.

Real designs also include source resistance and warm cable resistance, so a margin is needed. All figures here are example values; a qualified electrician must verify any real design against the maker's tables and local rules.
modules.example: Continue with the 0.72 ohm loop and a 230 V supply. Fault current is 230 ÷ 0.72 = about 319 A. Suppose the 16 A device needs about 10 times its rating, so 160 A, to trip instantly. Since 319 is above 160, it passes with a margin of about 2 times. Now try 6 mm² over 120 m: loop is 2 × 0.0225 × 120 ÷ 6 = 0.9 ohms, giving 230 ÷ 0.9 = 256 A. A 32 A device needing 320 A fails, since 256 is below 320.
modules.activity: Run the same check for 4 mm² over 60 m with a 20 A device needing 10 times its rating. State pass or fail and the margin.
modules.standard: Learner calculates fault current, compares with the trip level and states pass or fail.

modules.title: What sets the longest workable length
modules.intro: Four things set how long a run can be. Changing one of them is how you fix a run that fails.
points: Protective device type and rating: a lower trip level allows longer.
Supply voltage and temperature: warm cable has higher resistance.
Core count and how the cable is laid also affect the result.
modules.example: The failing 6 mm² run at 120 m gave 256 A against 320 A needed. Option one: move up to 10 mm². Loop is 2 × 0.0225 × 120 ÷ 10 = 0.54 ohms and fault current is 230 ÷ 0.54 = about 426 A. That passes. Option two: keep 6 mm² and ask for a device with a lower trip level, for example one needing 5 times its rating, so 160 A, and 256 passes. Option three: shorten the route to 80 m, giving 0.6 ohms and 383 A, which also passes. Three fixes, each with a cost.
modules.activity: For the failing run, list the three fixes. Choose one and say what extra it costs (money, space, or a different device).
modules.standard: Learner names the four factors and proposes at least two valid fixes with numbers.

modules.title: Voltage drop as a second check
modules.intro: A run can pass the fault check and still be poor, because a long cable also drops voltage under load. Both checks must pass.
points: Voltage drop is load current times loop resistance in this simple model.
Motors and electronics need voltage near their rating.
If either check fails, the run needs to be corrected by a qualified person before use.
modules.example: Take the 2.5 mm² 40 m run with 0.72 ohms loop resistance and a 20 A load. Drop is 20 × 0.72 = 14.4 V. As a share of 230 V that is 14.4 ÷ 230 = about 6.3 per cent. Many designs aim for a smaller share, so this run may be a concern for sensitive loads even though it passed the fault check. Moving to 4 mm² gives loop 0.45 ohms, drop 9 V, about 3.9 per cent. Check the allowed limit in the national wiring rules that apply where you work; a qualified electrician must confirm it.
modules.activity: Calculate voltage drop as a number and a percentage for a 10 A load on 60 m of 2.5 mm² cable. Say whether you would accept it without checking the local limit.
modules.standard: Learner computes drop in volts and per cent and keeps it as a separate check from fault current.

quiz.q: Why is the loop length twice the cable length?
quiz.a: Current goes out along one conductor and returns along another.

quiz.q: What is the loop resistance of 2.5 mm² copper over 40 m using 0.0225 ohm mm² per metre?
What happens to loop resistance if the conductor size is halved?
With a 0.72 ohm loop on 230 V, what is the fault current?
A 16 A device needs 160 A to trip instantly. Does a 319 A fault pass?
A 32 A device needs 320 A and the run gives 256 A. Pass or fail?
Name three ways to fix a run that fails the fault check.
quiz.a: Use a thicker cable, shorten the route, or use a device with a lower trip level.

quiz.q: What fault current does 10 mm² over 120 m give at 230 V?
A 20 A load on a 0.72 ohm loop. What is the voltage drop?
quiz.a: 14.4 V, about 6.3 per cent of 230 V.

quiz.q: Why check voltage drop separately from fault current?
quiz.a: A run can trip properly in a fault and still deliver too low a voltage under load.

ladder.title: L1 Basic: Long cable, weak fault
ladder.slide: Two cables of different lengths with arrows showing strong and weak current.
ladder.notes: Open with the idea that distance weakens the fault current. Keep it visual. No formulas yet.

ladder.title: L2 Explain: The loop
ladder.slide: Diagram of current going out along one conductor and back along another.
ladder.notes: Explain why loop length is double. Work 2 × 0.0225 × 40 ÷ 2.5 = 0.72 ohms on the board.

ladder.title: L3 Apply: Fault current
ladder.slide: Worked sum 230 ÷ 0.72 = 319 A next to a trip level of 160 A.
ladder.notes: Walk through pass. Then show the 6 mm² 120 m case at 256 A failing against 320 A. Remind learners these are rounded teaching figures.

ladder.title: L4 Analyse: Three fixes
ladder.slide: Table comparing 10 mm², lower trip device and a shorter route with resulting amps.
ladder.notes: Learners compare 426, 256 against 160, and 383 A. Discuss cost and practicality of each fix.

ladder.title: L5 Design: Pick a cable
ladder.slide: Brief: 90 m run, 230 V, 20 A device needing 200 A. Choose a size.
ladder.notes: Learners try sizes and show the working. Real designs use maker tables, and qualified people take the decisions.

ladder.title: L6 Evaluate: Voltage drop
ladder.slide: Same run with a 20 A load showing a 14.4 V drop and 6.3 per cent.
ladder.notes: Show that passing one check does not pass both. Ask what limit applies locally and who would know.

ladder.title: L7 Create: Check sheet
ladder.slide: Blank sheet with boxes for size, length, loop, fault current, trip level, drop, verdict.
ladder.notes: Learners build their own check sheet and test it on an invented run. Close by repeating that final design sits with qualified people and the local rules.

rubric.not_yet: Uses the cable length once, not doubled, or mixes units.
rubric.meets: Calculates loop resistance correctly with the working shown.
rubric.exceeds: Explains how length, size and temperature each move the result.

rubric.not_yet: Cannot compare fault current to the trip level.
rubric.meets: Calculates fault current and states pass or fail with a margin.
rubric.exceeds: Notes the limits of the simple model and asks for maker tables.

rubric.not_yet: Offers no fix or an untested one.
rubric.meets: Offers at least two fixes with checked numbers.
rubric.exceeds: Compares fixes by cost and practicality and picks one with a reason.

rubric.not_yet: Ignores voltage drop or implies anyone may change the circuit.
rubric.meets: Checks voltage drop separately and says qualified people finalise the design.
rubric.exceeds: Links the drop result to the needs of the load and the local limit.

jobs.what: Sizes cables and chooses protection so faults clear quickly and voltage stays healthy.
Prices cable runs and spots long routes that will need larger sizes.
Measures loop values on site and compares them with the design, following local rules.
Reviews layouts and makes sure cable routes and ratings match the design checks.
